截至2026年7月29日上午，中国这一轮灾情呈现出“台风连续登陆、雨带南北摆动、洪涝与山体滑坡叠加”的特点。受灾最严重、人员伤亡最集中的地区是广西、湖北、重庆和甘肃；浙江、河北、辽宁、吉林、广东等地则以大规模转移、城市内涝和基础设施损坏为主。
一、近几周主要灾情
时间及地区
主要灾害
最新公开伤亡及影响
7月3—9日：海南、广西
台风“美莎克”登陆海南后，其残余环流在广西形成极端降雨。南宁横州六蓝水库等出现漫顶、缺口，横州、宾阳、贵港、防城港、钦州等地发生洪水、内涝
广西39人死亡、9人失联；其中六蓝水库灾害26人死亡、7人失联。南宁市转移安置6.45万人，横州、宾阳多条道路、电力、通信受损。新华社通报
7月6—7日：湖北
黄冈、黄石、鄂州、咸宁遭遇雷暴大风和龙卷风，黄冈出现EF2级龙卷风
1.46万人受灾，11人死亡、1人失联、331人受伤；22间房屋倒塌、4,855间损坏。新华社通报
7月7日：甘肃陇南宕昌
突发山体滑坡，33名林业作业人员被困。该事件原因仍在调查，不能简单归因于暴雨
21人死亡、7人轻伤、5人未受伤。新华社通报
7月11—15日：浙江及华东、华北、东北
台风“巴威”先后登陆浙江玉环、乐清，并把大量水汽输送至河北、辽宁、吉林等地
浙江累计转移超过268万人，台州、温州出现风损、内涝、树木及设施损坏；未见浙江重大人员伤亡官方报告。河北宽城等地洪水，辽宁沈阳降雨破纪录；吉林多条河流超警、多个水库超汛限。新华社报道
7月17日：重庆彭水
连续强降雨后发生大型山体崩塌，十余栋住宅、商铺及一辆客运车被埋
截至7月28日，41人确认死亡、20人失联、10人受伤，仍在搜寻和身份鉴定。AP最新更新
7月26日：甘肃定西渭源
双石门景区短时强降雨引发山洪，露营、自驾游客被困
10人死亡、23人受伤，另有174人获救；305名消防救援人员参与救援。应急管理部
7月26日起：广东及华南、华中
第12号台风“红霞”登陆广东惠州惠东，影响汕尾、揭阳、惠州、河源、韶关、深圳，并向江西、湖南、湖北等地输送降雨
广东转移超过70万人；截至目前尚未公布大陆完整伤亡与直接经济损失。广东、江西、湖南等地多条河流超警。水利部通报
机械汇总上述有明确数字、并与暴雨或台风直接相关的四起主要伤亡事件——广西、湖北、重庆彭水、甘肃渭源——至少已有101人死亡、30人失联、364人受伤。这个数字不是官方全国总数：广西死亡与失联名册可能存在交叉，其他地方零散伤亡尚未完全纳入；甘肃宕昌山体滑坡的21名遇难者也未计入其中。
二、经济损失目前有多大
目前应急管理部尚未发布“2026年7月全国自然灾害汇总”，所以网上一些所谓“全国损失数字”并不完整。
较可靠的量化指标是：
 截至7月13日，广西、湖北、浙江等20个省区市，保险业累计接到近38万件报案，保险估损63.8亿元，已赔付28.9亿元；其中台风“巴威”估损5.4亿元。金融监管总局数据
 “红霞”影响广东后，截至7月27日，广东保险业接报20,005件，已经支付赔款约3,679万元；后续金额仍会上升。
 中央已紧急预拨1.8亿元，支持广东、福建、江西、湖南、辽宁、吉林六省抢险、人员安置、隐患排查及民房修复。应急管理部
 此外，国家发改委分别安排浙江1亿元、河北3,000万元、吉林3,000万元，支持道路、水利、学校、医院等恢复。这些是财政支持资金，不等于实际经济损失，而且可能与其他救灾资金部分重叠。
作为背景，2026年上半年洪涝和地质灾害已造成1,132.6万人次受灾、124人死亡失踪、直接经济损失338.7亿元；全部自然灾害直接损失421.4亿元。应急管理部上半年数据
三、未来一至三周风险
当前还没有完全结束。7月29日中央气象台继续发布暴雨黄色预警，重点包括广东、广西、湖北、四川、河南、河北、山东、吉林、黑龙江及内蒙古东北部；部分地区还可能出现山洪、滑坡、城市内涝、雷暴大风和冰雹。中央气象台最新预报
国家气候中心预计，“七下八上”期间仍可能有2—3个台风登陆或影响中国，其中可能有一个较强台风北上；京津冀、东北地区降雨偏多，华南和华东沿海仍是台风重点风险区。国家气候中心预测
四、最值得关注的商业与投资机会
我认为真正有持续性的机会不是短期囤积救灾物资，而是未来3—5年的“气候韧性基础设施”。
病险水库、堤坝与水利工程升级
广西水库险情会推动全国中小水库安全鉴定、除险加固、渗漏监测和数字化管理。机会包括水利EPC、坝体检测、传感器、无人机巡检、排涝泵站及长期运维。
城市排水与防内涝
沈阳、南宁、深圳等城市内涝暴露出排水标准不足。地下蓄洪空间、调蓄池、排水管网、泵站、挡水板、海绵城市和城市洪水数字孪生，可能成为地方专项债及中央预算投资重点。
地质灾害监测预警
重庆、甘肃连续滑坡会推动边坡雷达、InSAR卫星监测、北斗定位、雨量和土壤含水传感器、AI滑坡预警，以及景区、矿区、公路和铁路边坡监测。这个领域技术壁垒和后续服务收入相对较高。
应急装备与移动基础设施
大流量排涝泵、救援机器人、无人机、卫星通信终端、移动储能及发电机、应急净水设备、舟艇和临时安置设施，短期订单最直接，但收入通常随灾情波动。
灾后重建材料与工程
道路桥梁修复、管材、电缆、防水材料、预制建筑、通信基站和配电设备会受益。不过传统建筑材料竞争激烈、回款周期长，不一定等于好的股票投资。
农业恢复与智慧农业
受淹农田需要补种种子、农机、植保、动物防疫、农产品烘干及冷链；卫星遥感查勘、农业气象指数保险也会加快应用。
巨灾保险与气候金融
长期机会在巨灾保险、参数保险、农业气象保险和气候风险模型；但传统保险公司短期首先面对赔付增加，因此不能简单理解为“灾情越大，保险股越受益”。
从投资角度，我会优先选择“已有政府订单和运维收入”的水利数字化、监测预警、排涝设备公司，而不是单纯追逐水泥、建材等短期题材。筛选时重点看在手订单、应收账款回收、地方政府客户比例、现金流和真实防灾业务收入占比。
结合你在中国—阿联酋的资源，这里还有一个很好的跨境商业方向：把中国的“城市防内涝＋坡体监测＋移动排涝＋卫星通信＋保险风险模型”整合成一套解决方案，向阿联酋的市政部门、地产开发商、工业园区、机场和自由区输出。中国这轮灾情形成的技术升级，恰好可以转化成海湾国家应对突发暴雨的产品和案例。

Economy resilient, stronger momentum ahead - Chinadaily.com.cn

Economy resilient, stronger momentum ahead
By Yang Yaowu | China Daily | Updated: 2026-07-20 10:50
First, new growth drivers continued to upgrade manufacturing and optimize the structure of foreign trade. Production of high-tech and high-value-added products accelerated, with their share in exports continuing to increase. In the first half, value-added industrial output of enterprises above designated size grew 5.4 percent year-on-year, while value-added output of high-tech manufacturing rose 13.3 percent, outpacing the same period last year by 3.8 percentage points and accelerating 0.8 percentage point from the first quarter. Production of computers, communication equipment and other electronic products — as well as industrial robots — maintained rapid growth. High-tech manufacturing contributed nearly 40 percent of total industrial growth, gradually becoming a core driver of economic expansion.
The development of new growth drivers also promoted both higher-quality and faster growth in foreign trade. Merchandise exports reached $2.13 trillion in the first half, up 17.6 percent year-on-year, while imports totaled $1.55 trillion, rising 26.6 percent. Exports of mechanical and electrical products surged 24.5 percent, accounting for more than 60 percent of total exports. Driven by the global technology cycle, imports and exports of artificial intelligence-related products, including electronic components, computer parts, optical fiber and cables, grew by around 50 percent year-on-year. AI-related industrial chains, such as integrated circuits and computer components, have become an important pillar supporting export growth. As China continues to increase the supply of innovative products that meet the global trend toward digitalization and green development, it has further consolidated and expanded its diversified overseas markets. Trade with ASEAN, the European Union and Africa all recorded double-digit growth, while trade with Belt and Road partner countries increased by 14.8 percent, accounting for more than half of China's total foreign trade for the first time.
Second, the investment structure continued to improve, with greater emphasis placed on fostering future growth potential and improving people's well-being. Although overall fixed-asset investment growth moderated in the first half, investment in high-tech industries continued to grow steadily, while investment in intellectual property products accelerated further. Investment related to the six networks — water conservancy, new power grids, computing infrastructure, next-generation telecommunications, urban underground utilities and logistics — continued to expand, providing stronger support for long-term development capacity and public well-being.
Third, demand for services consumption grew steadily, while the potential of new forms of consumption continued to be unleashed. As living standards continue to improve, the rising share of services consumption reflects the natural evolution of China's economy and creates broader opportunities for foreign businesses seeking to expand in China. In the first half, retail sales of services increased 5.3 percent year-on-year, while spending on culture, sports and leisure services maintained rapid growth. Holiday travel, cultural performances and inbound tourism all recorded solid increases. At the same time, online, digital and green consumption emerged as new growth areas. Retail sales of high-energy efficiency household appliances continued to expand rapidly, while the retail penetration rate of new energy vehicles exceeded 60 percent for the third consecutive month, highlighting the continued release of new consumption potential.

The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 11.7% from 2026 to 2036.
North America dominates the global smart water management market, accounting for the largest share in 2026. This leadership is attributed to the early adoption of advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) and automated meter reading (AMR) technologies, strong regulatory oversight, and substantial government funding for water infrastructure modernization, including investments under the U.S. Bipartisan Infrastructure Law.
Asia-Pacific is projected to register the highest CAGR during the forecast period, driven by rapid urbanization, industrial growth, large-scale smart city initiatives, and increasing government investments in digital water infrastructure across China, India, Japan, and South Korea.
By offering, the hardware segment is expected to account for the largest share of the global smart water management market in 2026, driven by growing deployment of AMI/AMR meters, smart sensors, IoT-enabled field devices, and control systems.
By offering, the services segment is projected to register the fastest CAGR during the forecast period, as utilities and municipalities increasingly require system integration, data analytics, cybersecurity support, and managed services to optimize smart water investments.
By application, the water quality & quantity monitoring segment is expected to hold the largest share in 2026, reflecting growing regulatory requirements and the need for real-time monitoring to reduce water losses and ensure compliance.
By end user, the municipal utilities segment is expected to account for the largest share in 2026, driven by widespread adoption of digital water management solutions to improve distribution efficiency, reduce non-revenue water, and enhance service reliability.
Segments covered: offering, application, end user. Regions: North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific.
The growth of the smart water management market is driven by the increasing need to minimize water loss resulting from non-revenue water (NRW), the modernization and replacement of aging water infrastructure, and rising investment in digital water technologies. Capital flows into the broader water sector have strengthened in recent years. For instance, according to the White & Case LLP “Currents of Capital 2025” report, 30% of surveyed respondents deployed more than USD 500 million into the water sector in 2024, and a majority of organizations expected to increase investment levels in 2025 compared to the previous year. Government initiatives to integrate smart water management solutions into urban infrastructure programs, coupled with the proliferation of smart city projects globally, are also anticipated to create substantial growth opportunities for stakeholders in smart water management throughout the forecast period.
Smart water management solutions leverage advanced technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), digital twin modeling, cloud analytics, advanced metering infrastructure (AMI), and LPWAN (Low-Power Wide-Area Network) connectivity to enable real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, leak detection, and data-driven optimization of water distribution networks and treatment operations. The combination of these digital technologies with the urgent global need for sustainable water resource management, driven by accelerating water stress, stricter regulatory mandates, and the growing recognition of water as a strategic economic resource, is reshaping the water utility sector and creating significant demand for integrated smart water management platforms across residential, commercial, and industrial end users worldwide.
Smart water management (SWM) encompasses the integrated application of digital technologies, data analytics, and automation to optimize every stage of the water cycle, from source abstraction and treatment through distribution, consumption monitoring, leak detection, and wastewater management. SWM platforms integrate hardware components including smart meters (AMI and AMR), IoT-enabled sensors, smart pumps and drives, smart valves, and water controllers with software platforms for cloud-based and on-premise analytics, SCADA integration, digital twin modeling, asset management, geographic information systems (GIS), and customer engagement portals. These integrated systems enable water utilities, industrial operators, commercial facilities, and residential consumers to monitor water usage in real time, detect leaks and anomalies proactively, optimize pressure management, improve billing accuracy, and make data-driven decisions that enhance operational efficiency and resource sustainability.
The smart water management market is undergoing accelerated digital transformation driven by the combination of escalating water scarcity, aging water infrastructure, rising regulatory requirements, and the maturation of enabling technologies. In 2025, China invested a record USD 182.4 billion (1.28 trillion yuan) in the construction of water conservancy facilities, exceeding the trillion-yuan mark for the fourth consecutive year. In the U.S., the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law continues to direct more than USD 50 billion via the EPA toward improvements in drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater infrastructure, helping catalyze utility investment in modernization efforts such as smart metering, leak detection, and digital water management systems across North America. These substantial public investment programs are directly catalyzing procurement of smart metering, leak detection, and digital water management systems.
The ongoing transition from conventional mechanical meters and one-way automated meter reading (AMR) systems to advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) is a key trend in the global smart water management market. Unlike legacy systems, AMI enables two-way communication, interval-based consumption measurement, remote meter configuration, and real-time data transmission to utility control centers. This transition is allowing utilities to move from reactive billing models to proactive network management strategies.
AMI deployments now represent the dominant technology pathway for new smart water meter installations in developed markets. Utilities are increasingly prioritizing AMI to improve billing accuracy, reduce non-revenue water (NRW), detect customer-side leaks, enable time-of-use pricing structures, and enhance customer engagement through digital portals and mobile applications. The granular consumption data generated by AMI supports predictive maintenance and demand forecasting, improving operational efficiency across distribution networks.
As utilities seek to digitize water infrastructure while managing capital expenditure constraints, AMI and IoT-integrated smart metering systems are becoming foundational components of broader digital water strategies. This trend is expected to continue accelerating through 2036, driven by regulatory pressure to reduce water losses, improve transparency, and enhance resilience against climate-related water stress.
The growing integration of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and digital twin technology into smart water management platforms is transforming water utility operations from reactive, manual processes to proactive, data-driven management. Digital twins enable utilities to simulate outcomes, predict pipe failures, optimize pressure zones, and plan capital projects based on risk scores rather than asset age alone. Enterprise asset management modules integrated with hydraulic modeling engines predict pipe failures well ahead of visible leaks, reducing emergency repair expenditure significantly. AI algorithms applied to real-time sensor data from distribution networks can identify leak signatures, quantify non-revenue water losses, and prioritize intervention responses with a precision that is unachievable through conventional monitoring. Utilities implementing smart water systems with AI analytics achieve 15–30% reductions in water losses, yielding substantial operational savings. Shenzhen, China, has deployed IoT-enabled smart metering across over 80% of residential households, reducing NRW rates to approximately 6.2%.
Rising governmental initiatives to integrate smart water management into national infrastructure investment programs and the accelerating growth of smart city projects globally are creating significant large-scale deployment opportunities for smart water management technology and service providers. In the U.S., the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law’s water infrastructure provisions and the EPA’s WaterSense program are catalyzing municipal smart metering deployments and digital water system upgrades across hundreds of utilities. In Germany, the government’s Digital Strategy 2025 mandates a national rollout of smart meters to commercial and residential customers from 2025, creating a large addressable market for smart water metering providers. China continues to invest in water conservancy modernization, committing record capital to smart irrigation, urban water distribution digitization, and industrial water efficiency programs. Smart city projects across Asia-Pacific, the Middle East, and Europe are embedding smart water management as a core infrastructure component, thereby driving the growth of the overall smart water management market.
The U.S. smart water management market is projected to grow at a strong CAGR from 2026 to 2036, driven by the substantial federal funding provisions of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, the EPA’s expanded focus on water system cybersecurity and PFAS remediation, and the growing adoption of AMI metering, leak detection, and AI-powered distribution network analytics by municipal water utilities across the country. The U.S. is also a leader in smart water management innovation, with companies including IBM, Honeywell, Cisco, Mueller Water Products, Badger Meter, Trimble, HydroPoint, Sensus, Neptune Technology, and Itron headquartered or with major operations in the country. The hardware segment is expected to account for the largest share of the global smart water management market.
The significant market share of this segment is attributed to the increasing demand for automated meter reading for billing and analytical purposes, the widespread deployment of wireless communication-enabled smart meters capable of transmitting water usage data directly to central utility management systems, and the large installed base replacement cycle underway as utilities upgrade conventional mechanical meters to AMI and AMR devices.
However, the services segment is expected to witness the fastest CAGR during the forecast period.
Professional services, managed services, and outcome-based service contracts are growing at an accelerated pace as utilities recognize that the full operational and financial value of smart water investments is realized only when supported by embedded data science expertise, system integration capabilities, and ongoing change management support.
Vendors are increasingly offering multi-year platform agreements that bundle hardware, software licensing, connectivity, and guaranteed operational performance improvements, generating highly recurring and visible service revenue streams.
The water quality & quantity monitoring segment is expected to account for the largest share of the global smart water management market.
The large share of this segment is mainly attributed to the increasing deployment of IoT-enabled sensors for continuous real-time monitoring of water quality parameters, including physical, chemical, and microbial properties, across distribution networks, treatment plants, and industrial process water systems.
The leak detection application segment is expected to witness strong growth during the forecast period, driven by the growing financial imperative for utilities to reduce non-revenue water losses and the increasing sophistication of AI-powered acoustic leak detection, pressure transient analysis, and anomaly detection algorithms that can pinpoint leak locations in complex pipe networks with high accuracy.
The industrial segment is expected to account for the largest share of the global smart water management market.
The large market share of this segment is attributed to the widespread adoption of smart water management solutions across diverse industrial sectors such as manufacturing, agriculture, utilities, energy, mining, oil & gas, food & beverage, chemicals, and construction, which are deploying integrated IoT monitoring, real-time consumption analytics, and automated control systems to measure and manage water use at individual plant and process levels.
Industrial operators use smart water management platforms to reduce operational costs by optimizing water consumption, minimize regulatory compliance risk through automated effluent monitoring and reporting, identify process inefficiencies driving excess water usage, and trigger automated alerts when consumption or quality parameters deviate from established thresholds.
The commercial segment is expected to witness the fastest CAGR during the forecast period, driven by stringent regulations and mandates governing water usage and conservation in commercial buildings, retail facilities, healthcare campuses, and data centers, and by the growing adoption of smart water solutions to meet corporate sustainability, ESG reporting, and net-zero water targets.
Asia-Pacific is expected to register the fastest CAGR during the forecast period of 2026 to 2036.
The growth of smart water management market in this region is primarily attributed to the combination of rapidly expanding urban populations and industrial activity that are straining existing water infrastructure, ambitious national smart city programs in China, India, South Korea, Singapore, and Japan, and significant government investment in digital water infrastructure and water security.
China is a major driver of regional growth, with USD 182.4 billion invested in water conservancy facilities in 2025 and Shenzhen's deployment of IoT-enabled smart metering across over 80% of residential households achieving NRW rates of approximately 6.2%.
Japan's coordinated smart water metering pilots in Tokushima, Kumamoto, and Kyoto highlight national-level commitment to household demand optimization and distribution network digitization.
Singapore's PUB utility has achieved a 54.4% reduction in non-revenue water since 2010 and 750% increase in smart meter coverage since 2015, serving as a global benchmark for smart water management implementation.
South Korea and India are also high-growth markets, driven by smart city infrastructure investment and growing industrial water management requirements.

The long-term structural integrity of reservoir-dam systems is essential for ensuring water security, energy supply, and public safety. Underwater structural defects, driven by complex hydraulic and environmental conditions, pose growing threats to the safe operation of large dams. In recent decades, significant progress has been made in underwater inspection, defect detection, and repair technologies, offering viable alternatives to traditional drawdown-based maintenance. This review systematically synthesizes advances in underwater detection and rehabilitation technologies for reservoir-dam systems, focusing on inspection platforms, positioning and navigation methods, defect identification techniques, and underwater repair materials. It critically examines key challenges, including limited transferability of marine-derived technologies, environmental interference, cumulative operational errors, and real-world applicability. This paper further categorizes existing technologies by maturity and proposes problem-oriented research directions to support the development of intelligent, reliable, and field-deployable systems for underwater defect management in large dams.
Global population growth, rapid urbanization, and sustained socio-economic development have substantially increased water and electricity demands. Concurrently, global efforts to address climate change and enhance disaster resilience have created new opportunities for hydropower expansion 1 . According to the International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD) 2 , the total number of large dams worldwide reached 62,339 by 2024. China leads globally in the number of high dams and reservoirs with 683 dams exceeding 70 m in height, including 244 above 100 m and 23 surpassing 200 m 3 . However, environmental changes, extreme operating conditions, seismic activity, and geological hazards have resulted in increasing structure aging and performance degradation 4 , 5 , 6 . Consequently, numerous reservoir dams face potential safety risks and structural deficiencies 7 . If left unaddressed, these conditions can lead to catastrophic failures such as dam breaches, uncontrolled flooding, and significant disruptions to water and energy supply, resulting in immense economic losses, environmental damage, and potential loss of life. The escalating risks underscore the urgent need for advanced, reliable, and cost-effective underwater inspection and repair technologies to ensure the long-term safety and operational continuity of these critical infrastructures. The complicated operational environments of these systems create significant challenges for underwater inspection, repair, and safety diagnostics. While some defects can be addressed through underwater interventions and routine maintenance, others necessitate costly dewatering procedures. Dam structures require interdisciplinary approaches to underwater inspection and repair due to their diversity, varying depths, complex geometries, and heterogeneous defect profiles. In recent years, underwater inspection and reinforcement technologies have emerged as critical priorities in hydraulic engineering 8 , 9 , 10 . These challenges underscore the necessity for advances in precise detection techniques and rapid safety diagnostic methods for underwater defects in reservoir–dam systems essential for ensuring long-term dam safety 11 , 12 . Critically, effective underwater defect rehabilitation directly supports key UN Sustainable Development Goals by ensuring water security through contamination prevention and reliable supply (SDG 6), fostering resilient infrastructure innovation for renewable hydropower (SDG 9), protecting urban communities from catastrophic failures (SDG 11), and enabling climate adaptation/mitigation via flood control and carbon-neutral energy (SDG 13) 13 .
Given the rapid advancements in this interdisciplinary field, a comprehensive review that synthesizes current strategies, assesses their strengths and limitations, and identifies critical challenges is both timely and essential to guide future research and development. This paper presents a comprehensive review of underwater detection, repair, and retrofitting technologies for reservoir–dam systems.
Incidents threatening reservoir-dam safety are a global concern. Data from the US, China, and Europe highlight that defects occur across dams of all types and ages 14 (Fig. 1 ). The high cost of rehabilitation underscores the need for proactive maintenance 15 . Unlike marine environments, reservoir-dam systems present unique challenges: narrow valleys affecting GPS signals, extreme hydrostatic pressures at high dams ( > 100 m), and complex underwater currents near intakes. These factors necessitate specialized equipment distinct from standard oceanographic tools. Traditionally, underwater inspections and repairs have involved draining reservoir and conducting manual inspections to identify structural defects 16 . While this approach was standard practice, it presents significant disadvantages: it is time-consuming, wastes water, and poses risks of environmental pollution and ecological harm 17 , 18 . Numerous existing high dams, particularly those in the 300 m class, lack emergency drawdown facilities or required conditions for drawdown 19 , resulting in limited safety assurance capabilities.

Despite the clear and pressing need for underwater inspection and repair technologies in reservoir-dam systems, the actual implementation of such operations remains fraught with scientific and engineering difficulties. The complexity of the underwater environment, coupled with the diversity of structural forms and defect types, imposes significant constraints on the performance of existing detection and intervention systems. To guide future technological development and field deployment, it is essential to systematically analyze the key challenges that currently limit the effectiveness, reliability, and safety of underwater operations 20 , 21 . The following section outlines four major categories of challenges, ranging from theoretical model transferability to the propagation of cumulative operational errors, which collectively hinder the advancement of underwater defect management in dam engineering.
Development of underwater operational technologies and equipment initially emerged from the marine engineering sector 22 , primarily supporting ocean observation, offshore oil and gas extraction, deep-sea mineral mining, marine scientific research, and military applications 23 , 24 . These activities involve substantial technical requirements, investment, risks, and returns. Gradually, the application scope has expanded to shipbuilding 25 , inland navigation 26 , water conservancy and hydropower 7 , and nuclear power 27 , advancing toward lightweight, modular, and intelligent systems. However, the operational conditions for underwater inspection, repair, and reinforcement in reservoir-dam systems differ significantly from marine environment (See detail in Fig. 2 ). Technologies developed for marine purposes cannot be directly transferred. Notable distinctions include: (1) Reservoir valleys generally feature substantially narrower surface areas compared to open oceans. Large river valleys typically span several hundred meters, while mountainous gorges may measure only tens of meters, affecting underwater inspection equipment positioning accuracy 28 , 29 , 30 . (2) Reservoir acoustical environments are complicated by U- shaped or V-shaped valleys, complex hydraulic structures, uneven reservoir bottoms, and siltation 31 . These factors significantly affect acoustic wave reflection, diminishing the effectiveness 32 , 33 . (3) Unlike the high-visibility of marine waters, reservoirs typically contain turbid waters with poor visibility. Moreover, bed-load and suspended sediments increase noise and signal attenuation in both acoustic and optical detection systems 16 , 20 , 21 . In addition, high-flow velocity zones near hydraulic structures threaten detection equipment safety 34 .
The schematic contrasts open-water and reservoir settings in terms of water-area characteristics, terrain, visibility, flow conditions, equipment transport and working environment.
The aquatic environment is further impacted by unsteady and multiphase flows, which modify medium parameters and attenuate detection signals. Underwater acoustic-optical imaging face challenges from external noise, clutter interference, and internal system or quantization noise, creating complex perturbations across acoustic, optical, and hydrodynamic fields. This results in significant signal-to-noise ratio fluctuations; in some cases, signals become completely obscured by noise, degrading imaging quality and rendering targets undetectable 35 , 36 . Most underwater defects in hydraulic structures initiate or manifest at the surface before progressing inward. These features often concealed by biofouling are typically subtle and unstructured, leading to significant uncertainty in defect characterization 37 . Moreover, under the influence of various natural and anthropogenic influences, dam service behavior exhibits characteristics such as multi-source uncertainty, nonlinearity, and temporal variability 38 , 39 . The evolution mechanisms and failure modes of underwater structural defects are intricate. Current research inadequately addresses correlations between potential hazards and lacks clarity regarding topological relationships among underwater defects. This is exacerbated by insufficient deep-water data fusion methods and continued reliance on single-method diagnostics 40 , 41 resulting in ambiguity in structural performance assessment(Fig. 3 ). Moreover, complex flow regimes, poor water quality, and intricate structural configurations within reservoir-dam systems present significant challenges for underwater inspection, repair, and reinforcement operations. Manual operations are often constrained by diver endurance and expertise 42 . Divers encounter risks from water pressure, strong currents, and low temperatures 43 , making safety, efficiency, and consistency difficult to maintain. Meanwhile, underwater vehicle operations face limitations in perception, precision, and autonomous decision-making capabilities 44 , 45 . These constraints impede robotic task refinement, and current level of automation and intelligence remains insufficient to replace human involvement in repair and reinforcement tasks 46 , 47 . The complexity of the reservoir-dam environment amplifies operational uncertainty and difficulty, making it impossible to fully address hidden defects. Therefore, hazard detection and interpretation remain significant challenges. Research and development specifically adapted to reservoir environmental conditions and boundary constraints are urgently needed. Prior objectives should include enhancing detection speed and accuracy, reducing computational and communication costs, and simplifying model complexity.
The framework links data acquisition and collation with underwater inspection, preprocessing, feature extraction, diagnosis and evaluation, and disposal or repair measures.
Various types of errors can significantly impact on underwater inspection, repair, and reinforcement operations, affecting their accuracy and effectiveness. These errors primarily manifest in four categories, as depicted in Fig. 4 for details.
Physical entity geometric errors: Complex external environments and structural behavior of the reservoir–dam system can lead to structural deformation in the physical geometry of hydraulic structures during long-term operation. Such deformation creates discrepancies between actual dimensions and measured results 48 , 49 , deviating from original design and construction data. Consequently, relying exclusively on construction drawings for underwater operations fails to meet precision requirements. Additionally, the inherent accuracy limitations of inspection equipment contribute to geometric measurement inaccuracies 50 , 51 .
Interactive timing errors during operational process mapping: Timing errors refer to data distortions resulting from desynchronization during data acquisition, processing, and transmission. These errors may arise from imprecise device clocks, signal transmission delays, or inconsistent data processing speeds 52 . Inadequate clock synchronization between different devices—or between underwater units and shore-based systems—combined with network latency and signal transmission uncertainties, can also introduce errors during data exchange 53 . In complex underwater operations requiring multiple devices working in coordination, timing errors can disrupt task sequencing 54 , 55 , compromising the continuity and effectiveness of the overall workflow.
Mutual feedback errors between underwater operational equipment and defects: Due to the variability of underwater terrain and structural complexity, mutual feedback errors mainly appear as positioning errors 56 , 57 . Positioning systems in underwater equipment, including GPS, long/short/ultra-short baseline systems, and inertial navigation systems, face limitation from complex hydraulic structures, uneven reservoir bottom topography, and siltation 58 . During multi-equipment, multi-scenario, and multi-mission underwater inspection and repair operations, cumulative error effects 59 may result in relative positioning deviations between sequential operational points.
Underwater environmental effect errors: The distinctive characteristics of underwater environments, such as light scattering and absorption, acoustic wave propagation characteristics 60 , and variations in temperature and pressure, result in uneven propagation of acoustic and optical waves used by different imaging methods 61 . This causes energy scattering, phase shifts, and reflection and diffraction across different media, ultimately reducing accuracy and reliability of detection data 16 . Furthermore, the complex and dynamic nature of underwater environments can adversely affect operational equipment and repair materials, increasing operational difficulty and uncertainty, thereby reducing the precision of underwater operations.
The diagram relates physical-entity geometric errors, interactive timing errors, mutual-feedback errors and underwater-environment effects to their causes, propagation mechanisms and operational consequences.
These four types of errors can be further categorized into systematic, measurement, positioning, environmental, human, and random errors. Systematic, measurement, and positioning errors typically have greater impact on outcomes and should be controlled through the usage of high-precision equipment, accurate calibration, and optimized workflows. While random and environmental errors remain unavoidable, they can be mitigated through repeated measurements, data filtering, and other techniques. Human errors require minimization through standardized procedures and strict operational protocols.
Although substantial advances have been achieved in underwater detection, positioning, and repair technologies for reservoir–dam systems, translating these developments into reliable large-scale engineering practice remains challenging 3 , 62 . The accuracy and reliability of landslide displacement predictions are critical to disaster early warning systems; however, most current research focuses on improving numerical precision while overlooking the potentially severe consequences of displacement underestimation. This paper proposes a landslide displacement prediction method that integrates a risk-aversion mechanism. In this approach, double exponential smoothing is employed to capture long-term trend changes in landslide displacement, and a hybrid model combining Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBOOST) is developed to characterize periodic displacement fluctuations. To address the risk of underestimation, a loss function incorporating a penalty factor is designed, and a constraint mechanism is introduced to adjust periodic displacement predictions toward a higher confidence interval. The predicted trend and periodic displacement components are then superimposed to generate a complete cumulative displacement forecast. In an empirical evaluation using the Dayangshan landslide in Suzhou, the proposed risk-averse prediction method not only maintains high predictive accuracy but also significantly reduces the rate of displacement underestimation, enabling dynamic and adaptive optimization of early warning strategies and risk control.
Landslide disasters occur with high frequency, exhibit dense spatial distribution, affect wide areas, and cause severe damage ( Liu X. et al., 2025 ; KC et al., 2024 ; Titus et al., 2023 ). Slope instability not only leads to ecological degradation but also results in substantial economic losses ( Cukur et al., 2025 ). Accurately predicting horizontal displacement changes in landslides can effectively mitigate disaster risks and has emerged as a cost-effective and practical strategy for disaster prevention and mitigation ( Liu H. et al., 2025 ; Wang Y. F. et al., 2025 ).
The horizontal displacement of landslides is highly complex, and its prediction remains a core challenge in natural hazard research ( Duan et al., 2023 ; Achu et al., 2025 ). As a typical nonlinear dynamical system, landslide movement is influenced by multiple coupled factors, including geological structure, topography, and human engineering activities ( Alcántara-Ayala, 2025 ). At present, research on landslide displacement prediction primarily emphasizes the quantitative assessment of point prediction accuracy, yet generally neglects the stochastic variability of prediction outcomes and its impact on overall system risk ( Wang et al., 2022 ). Traditional evaluation systems usually use indicators such as root mean square error or mean absolute error to measure model performance, but such methods cannot reflect the fluctuation characteristics of the predicted value within the confidence interval, and the risk loss is not included in the optimization objective ( Maghfuri and Kuku, 2025 ). For instance, in a landslide displacement prediction scenario, if a model outputs a displacement value of 0.9 m while the actual monitored value is 1.0 m, the absolute error is only 0.1 m. Nevertheless, such underestimation may mislead decision-makers into perceiving the landslide as stable, potentially delaying necessary engineering interventions and ultimately leading to sudden instability under critical conditions. The core issue underlying such underestimation events is that traditional accuracy metrics reflect only numerical discrepancies between predicted and observed values, without quantifying how prediction uncertainty propagates into landslide risk decision-making ( Parvathareddy et al., 2025 ).
The essence of a risk-aversion strategy lies in reducing the likelihood of risk occurrence or mitigating potential losses through proactive intervention ( Huff et al., 2022 ). In the context of landslide displacement prediction, risk aversion does not simply imply conservative predictions; rather, it involves introducing probabilistic forecasting frameworks—such as Bayesian neural networks or quantile regression—to transform displacement predictions into probability distribution estimates. These estimates can then be combined with risk matrix methods to evaluate the probability of landslide instability under different forecast confidence levels ( Li Y. et al., 2021 ). Fundamentally, this risk-based decision-making paradigm shifts the approach from “post-event remediation” to “pre-event control” through proactive intervention, thereby avoiding the “catastrophic underestimation trap” that traditional precision-oriented methods may encounter ( Ronco et al., 2023 ). Recently, the concept of risk aversion has generated considerable research interest, akin to a stone cast into the ocean of academic and applied inquiry ( Halter et al., 2025 ). Numerous researchers and industry experts have explored effective risk-aversion pathways and strategies ( Pugliese et al., 2021 ). As research has deepened, risk aversion has successfully crossed disciplinary boundaries and found wide application in structural prediction across various fields. Whether in the financial sector’s efforts to hedge against market volatility and forecast economic structures, or in engineering construction’s attempts to evade potential risks and predict structural stability, risk aversion plays a vital role in providing more reliable safeguards for development across domains ( Allioui and Mourdi, 2023 ; Okoroafor et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2024 ). In recent years, time series prediction methods based on signal decomposition (such as VMD) and state space models (such as Mamba) have demonstrated excellent performance in complex system modeling, providing a new research perspective for landslide displacement prediction ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Wang C. et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ).
Currently, research on risk aversion in landslide displacement forecasting is evolving along two main trajectories. The first trajectory centers on probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty quantification, employing methods such as Bayesian frameworks, quantile regression, and Conformal Prediction. These approaches characterize uncertainty by outputting prediction intervals or full probability distributions, thereby providing standardized theoretical tools for decision-making based on risk matrices ( Li F. et al., 2021 ). The second trajectory focuses on improving the accuracy of deterministic point forecasts, using loss functions like mean squared error that typically penalize overestimation and underestimation equally, without integrating specific risk-aversion preferences into the model optimization objectives. Consequently, within the paradigm of deterministic point forecasting, research remains insufficient on how to proactively and directly mitigate specific risks arising from systematic underestimation through redesigning loss functions. The methodological framework in this regard requires further enrichment and development. The aim of this paper is to address this gap by proposing a novel deterministic point forecasting method that incorporates a risk-aversion mechanism. In addition, the data driven technique as a new research method, while in other areas show the excellent performance, but in the complex landslide risk assessment system, its application is still in the exploratory stage ( Bao et al., 2022 ). The purpose of this paper is to reduce the underestimation of the prediction results caused by data uncertainty and model limitations in the process of landslide displacement prediction. Therefore, this paper proposes to construct a hybrid model based on support vector machine and extreme gradient boosting algorithm, which integrates the advantages of the two models to improve the prediction accuracy and avoid risks. Taking the Dayangshan landslide in Suzhou as a specific case, the application effect of the hybrid model method in the actual landslide displacement prediction and risk assessment is empirically analyzed and verified.
Double exponential smoothing (DES) is a method that applies exponential smoothing a second time to the initially smoothed values ( Kahraman and Akay, 2023 ; Rabbani et al., 2021 ). It cannot be used independently for prediction; rather, it must be combined with single exponential smoothing to establish a mathematical model for forecasting. For initial value determination, when observations exhibit a stable trend, the first data point can generally be used directly as the initial value. If the change trend of the observed value fluctuates, the average value of n data should be used as the initial value to reduce the impact of the initial value on the smooth value. The second exponential smoothing method essentially takes the weighted average of the historical data as the forecast result of the future time. It has the advantages of simple calculation, less sample requirement, stronger adaptability and more stable results. For this study, Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBOOST) were selected as the base models for constructing a hybrid predictor. This choice is primarily motivated by the following three considerations, which align closely with the objectives and constraints of this research.
The primary contribution of this paper lies in proposing and validating a general risk-aversion-embedded framework for landslide displacement forecasting (including temporal decomposition, hybrid architecture, and asymmetric loss functions), rather than conducting a comparative analysis of different base forecasting model architectures. As classic and powerful machine learning models, SVR and XGBOOST have been extensively validated for their effectiveness and robustness across various nonlinear regression tasks. They provide a reliable and reproducible baseline performance for verifying the proposed framework please see the Figure 1 .
The acquisition of landslide monitoring data is costly, and long-term, high-frequency, high-quality samples are often limited. While deep learning models (such as LSTM, GRU, or Transformer) possess strong representational capabilities, their full performance potential typically depends on large-scale training data. With limited samples, they are prone to overfitting, and their training processes are computationally complex. In contrast, SVR and XGBOOST generally demonstrate better sample efficiency and robustness on small-to-medium-sized datasets, with faster training and inference speeds. This aligns more closely with the computational efficiency and deployment practicality requirements of real-world monitoring systems.
Compared to complex deep learning “black boxes,” SVR and XGBOOST offer relatively better model interpretability (e.g., feature importance analysis in XGBOOST), helping engineering personnel understand model decisions and enhancing the method’s credibility and practicality. Furthermore, it is particularly emphasized that the proposed risk-aversion framework is model-agnostic. Its core concepts (decomposition, hybridization, asymmetric loss) can naturally be integrated with any modern forecasting model, such as LSTM or Transformer. This work uses classic models to validate the framework’s effectiveness, laying a solid foundation for future integration and optimization of more advanced deep learning architectures within this framework.
SVR and XGBOOST are both well-established prediction models in landslide displacement forecasting ( Sahin, 2023 ). SVR is developed from the Support Vector Machine (SVM). The basic idea of SVR is to map training data from the input space to a high-dimensional feature space via a kernel function and then construct a separating hyperplane with maximum margin in that feature space. The goal of regression problems is to determine a function that accurately estimates future values ( Han et al., 2021 ). XGBOOST (Extreme Gradient Boosting) is an efficient gradient boosting decision tree algorithm widely used in machine learning tasks on structured data ( Shi et al., 2022 ). XGBOOST significantly improves prediction performance by integrating multiple weak learners (decision trees) and gradually optimizing the model through gradient boosting. The core idea is to iteratively train a series of tree models, with each tree committed to correcting the prediction errors of the previous tree, ultimately obtaining a strong prediction model through weighted summation ( Xu et al., 2022 ). Therefore, this paper develops a hybrid model, which can maintain the positive part of each modeling method and prevent the problem of diminishing marginal utility of simple prediction model. To clarify the positioning of the method proposed in this paper, it is essential to articulate its fundamental distinction from existing risk-aversion approaches, such as Bayesian or quantile regression methods. The latter inherently belong to the “probabilistic forecasting” paradigm, whose core lies in quantifying uncertainty (by outputting prediction intervals or distributions), after which decision-makers must incorporate external risk models for subsequent analysis. In contrast, the method proposed herein falls under the “risk-adjusted point forecasting” paradigm. The key differences are as follows.
Traditional point forecasts minimize symmetric loss functions, whereas this study designs an asymmetric penalizing loss function ( Equation 6 ) that internalizes the risk preference of “reducing underestimation” directly into the optimization objective during model training.
Probabilistic methods output information (distributions/intervals) that describe uncertainty, leading to a relatively indirect decision-making pathway. The method proposed here directly outputs a single, safety-adjusted forecast value—shifted toward the conservative side (i.e., less prone to underestimation). This results in a more direct decision-making pathway, aiming to provide a reference point with a built-in safety margin for binary warning decisions, such as whether to trigger an alarm.
Probabilistic methods excel at comprehensively characterizing uncertainty but may demand more data and computational resources. The approach presented here offers a lightweight, interpretable solution for achieving risk aversion in scenarios that prioritize decision efficiency, operate under resource constraints, or favor the use of point forecasts. The two paradigms emphasize different aspects and complement each other.
Accordingly, the penalization mechanism proposed in this paper aims to address the risk of underestimation within the point forecasting paradigm.

In geotechnical engineering, the Factor of Safety (FoS) is a core design threshold for assessing slope stability. By analogy, r can be viewed as a “conservativeness coefficient” introduced into the forecasting model. A larger value of r leads to more conservative model outputs (i.e., higher predicted values and a lower risk of underestimation). The determination of r can be linked to engineering safety standards.
